tldr: Using reinforcement learning and three key innovations, this study achieves full sprinting at over 25 km/h (7.14 m/s) and high-speed aggressive cornering with up to 25° trunk lean on a full-scale humanoid, deployed zero-shot from simulation to the real robot.
hero_caption: Sprinting and aggressive cornering in simulation (Gazebo) and on the real humanoid robot. The top two rows show powerful sprinting at 6.5 m/s, while the bottom two rows demonstrate dynamic aggressive cornering at 5.5 m/s with an inward body lean of over 25 degrees.
overview:
Enabling a humanoid robot to sprint at the top speed of track-and-field athletes while maintaining human-like, natural motion has long been a dream. However, pushing past 14 km/h (around 4 m/s) brings three fatal bottlenecks that are invisible at walking speeds. First, periodic violent foot impacts produce severe yaw-rate oscillations in the body; a flat multi-layer perceptron (MLP) that simply concatenates state histories fails at state estimation. Second, standard turning commands based on yaw-rate tracking rewards fight these natural oscillations, forcing the robot to either slow down or give up turning. Third, training multiple skills such as walking and sprinting simultaneously with an Adversarial Motion Prior (AMP) confuses the discriminator, causing subtle skills like in-place turning to collapse into a static stance (mode collapse).

To solve this challenge, the authors introduced three targeted approaches. First, proprioceptive history is processed using a causal multi-head attention (MHA) module, extracting key gait phases and dynamic structures out of intense high-frequency vibrations. Second, abandoning direct tracking of oscillatory high-frequency yaw rates, they designed a heading-direction reward that tracks only the direction of the base translational velocity vector. This unlocks aggressive cornering without suppressing the natural gait-induced torso swaying. Third, they introduced skill-conditioned multi-adversarial-motion-prior (MAMP) discriminators, separating style evaluation across commanded skills to preserve fidelity from low-speed motions up to extreme sprinting.

Evaluation was conducted on a 17-DoF full-scale humanoid (1.8 m tall) in both simulation and real-world experiments. In a 100-meter dash on a standard running track, the real robot set a remarkable record of 7.14 m/s (around 25.7 km/h) average speed, and demonstrated aggressive high-speed turning with bank angles exceeding 25 degrees, all via zero-shot transfer without real-robot fine-tuning.
contributions: Systematically analyzed unique failure modes in ultra-high-speed bipedal sprinting (above 4 m/s), including severe proprioceptive high-frequency oscillations and turning reward conflicts.
Proposed a heading-direction reward that supervises only low-frequency velocity directions, enabling agile high-speed cornering accompanied by spontaneous inward trunk leaning (banking).
Adopted a causal multi-head attention (MHA) history encoder, drastically boosting dynamic stability during aggressive locomotion without increasing model capacity.
Introduced skill-conditioned Multi-AMP discriminators to prevent mode collapse across vastly different speed regimes (stand, in-place turn, walk, sprint), seamlessly unifying them in a single policy.
Demonstrated 7.14 m/s average sprinting speed in a real-world 100m dash and aggressive cornering on a full-scale humanoid via zero-shot transfer from simulation.

sections.heading: Why Can't Humanoids Sprint at Full Speed While Turning?
sections.summary: Sprinting on a full-scale humanoid causes high-frequency yaw oscillations from ground impacts, leading to state estimation failure, reward conflict during turning, and multi-skill mode collapse. This work builds a control framework that resolves all three, achieving >7 m/s sprinting and aggressive cornering on a real robot.
sections.details:
Recent research has achieved high-speed straight-line running on bipedal robots, but many of these gaits involve unnatural torso postures or flailing arms, far from the grace of human sprinters. Conversely, imitation learning frameworks like Adversarial Motion Prior (AMP) produce natural human-like motions, but have mostly been limited to low-to-medium speeds without high-speed agile cornering.

Why is it so difficult to combine top speed with natural agility? Pushing past 14 km/h (around 4 m/s) triggers three simultaneous high-speed failure modes:

- (i) Periodic foot impacts violently shake the torso, burying proprioceptive feedback (gyros and encoders) in high-frequency noise. Conventional flat-history MLPs (which simply flatten the observation history) cannot resolve critical temporal structures such as gait phases and contact timings, leading to state estimation failure.
- (ii) During running, the human trunk naturally sways left and right (yaw oscillation) to counteract leg swing momentum. Conventional yaw-rate tracking rewards penalize this natural swaying as tracking error, compelling reinforcement learning to decelerate or abandon turning altogether.
- (iii) When learning multiple skills—standing, in-place turning, walking, sprinting—with a single shared AMP discriminator, the discriminator only evaluates whether a motion looks like *any* reference clip. Consequently, subtle motions without translational velocity, such as in-place turning, degenerate into a static stance (mode collapse).

This paper proposes three clear solutions: (i) a causal multi-head attention (MHA) history encoder, (ii) a heading-direction reward tracking translational velocity vectors while ignoring high-frequency torso oscillations, and (iii) skill-conditioned Multi-AMP discriminators that separate evaluations per commanded skill. As a result, a 17-DoF full-scale humanoid achieves an average speed of 7.14 m/s in a real 100m sprint and executes high-speed aggressive cornering, both in simulation and real-world deployment.

sections.heading: Evolution of Adversarial Motion Priors and Attention Architectures
sections.summary: The paper surveys prior work across adversarial imitation learning (AMP), Transformer-based history encoders, and high-speed bipedal locomotion. Existing methods focus on medium-speed robustness or full-body tracking, leaving the coupled challenges of ultra-high-speed sprinting and aggressive turning unsolved.
sections.details:
This work builds on major advances in RL-based motion generation and policy architectures.

First is the lineage of Adversarial Motion Priors (AMP). AMP provides a powerful framework to autonomously discover natural motion styles from motion capture data without handcrafted gait rewards. While Multi-AMP variants have been explored for quadruped robots to handle multiple styles, no previous work has unified behaviors from standing up to sprinting at over 25 km/h conditioned explicitly on policy-level skill commands.

Second is the architectural evolution of observation history encoders. Flat-history MLPs have long dominated robot locomotion, but Transformer and attention mechanisms are rapidly gaining traction. Prior studies have shown that causal self-attention over proprioceptive history improves tracking of high-dimensional reference trajectories.

Third is the progress in sim-to-real transfer for bipeds like Cassie and outdoor humanoid locomotion and parkour. However, these works target obstacle traversal and high robustness at low-to-moderate speeds, leaving untouched the system-level challenge investigated here: severe high-frequency noise and turning-reward conflicts arising at extreme sprinting velocities.

captions.F2: Overview of the proposed system architecture. (1) Top: The MHA Actor summarizes the past T frames of proprioceptive history via causal self-attention, combining it with current velocity and skill commands to output target joint positions. (2) Bottom left: Skill-conditioned Multi-AMP discriminators provide independent style rewards matching the commanded skill. (3) Bottom right: The heading-direction reward evaluates the low-frequency direction of translational velocity instead of oscillatory yaw rate.

sections.heading: Three Core Technologies Enabling Sprinting and Aggressive Cornering
sections.summary: The authors construct a training pipeline integrating an MHA history encoder, a heading-direction reward, and skill-conditioned Multi-AMP. Operating without an explicit state estimator, the policy maps raw onboard sensor history and commands directly to target joint positions via end-to-end PPO.
sections.details:
The complete framework is summarized in Figure F2. Formulated as a discrete-time Markov Decision Process running at 50 Hz (every 0.02 s), it consists of the following key designs:

### 3.1 Problem Formulation
The policy receives a 7D command vector $\mathbf{c}_t \in \mathbb{R}^7$ (velocity commands $v_x, v_y, \omega_z$ plus a 4D one-hot skill label for stand, turn-in-place, walk, and sprint) alongside current proprioception $\mathbf{p}_t \in \mathbb{R}^{56}$ (base angular velocity, Euler angles, joint positions/velocities, and previous action). A history of the past $T=10$ frames is maintained. The policy output $\mathbf{a}_t \in \mathbb{R}^{17}$ specifies target joint angles, converted to torques by low-level PD controllers.

### 3.2 Multi-Head Attention (MHA) Actor
The past $T$ frames of proprioceptive history pass through a 1-layer, 2-head causal self-attention module (Transformer encoder). Mean-pooling across the temporal dimension yields a 128-dimensional dynamic summary vector, which is concatenated with the command embedding and fed to the Actor MLP. Remarkably, this MHA Actor contains roughly 3.6% fewer parameters than a standard flat MLP. Performance gains stem entirely from the inductive bias of temporal attention rather than model bloat.

### 3.3 Heading-Direction Reward
This is perhaps the most intuitive design insight. When forward speed exceeds $v_{\min} = 2.0\,\mathrm{m/s}$, the policy switches off the conventional yaw-rate $\omega_z$ tracking reward, enabling an alignment reward based on $e_{\text{align}} = 1 - \hat{\mathbf{v}}_t \cdot \hat{\mathbf{n}}_t$ between the base velocity unit vector $\hat{\mathbf{v}}_t$ and the target direction $\hat{\mathbf{n}}_t$. Because translational velocity is the time-integral of contact forces, lateral oscillations from alternating leg impacts cancel out within a stride, preserving only the smooth low-frequency heading. Free from instantaneous yaw constraints, the robot naturally adopts a deep inward trunk lean to carve tight turns.

### 3.4 Skill-Conditioned Multi-AMP
Four independent discriminators $D_i$ are instantiated for each skill. When 'sprint' is commanded, only the sprint discriminator updates and provides style rewards. To stabilize training at extreme velocities, the team adopted Wasserstein GAN loss, $\tanh$ score bounding, non-negative exponential reward mapping (preventing early episode termination from negative rewards), and dual gradient penalties ($R_1 + R_2$ regularization).

### 3.5 Training and Sim-to-Real Pipeline
PPO training was conducted in IsaacLab on 8 NVIDIA RTX 4090 GPUs using $4096 \times 8$ parallel environments. Domain randomizations include friction coefficients, base mass, center-of-mass positions, and motor latency (0–20 ms). The trained policy was exported as an ONNX model for zero-shot deployment on the real robot.

sections.heading: 25.7 km/h Real-World 100m Sprint! Ablations Reveal the Core Modules
sections.summary: Through rigorous benchmarks in Gazebo and Isaac Lab alongside a real 100m track dash, the proposed method achieved 7.14 m/s average speed and aggressive turning leaning over 25 degrees. Ablation experiments verified the necessity of each architectural component.
sections.details:
Evaluation was performed on a 1.8m, 17-DoF humanoid under standardized protocols (step acceleration tests, high-speed turning tests) and real-world track experiments.

### 4.1 Main Results and Ablation Setups
The proposed approach was benchmarked against flat MLP, GRU, LSTM, and a prior estimator-based baseline (HIM+MLP) under identical training conditions.

### 4.2 History Encoder Comparison (E1)
In step acceleration tests to 6.5 m/s, MHA, GRU, LSTM, and HIM all tracked the target, generalizing 18% beyond the training curriculum limit (5.5 m/s). Only the flat MLP saturated around 6.0 m/s. For straight-line running, any encoder capturing temporal structures proved effective. However, the high-speed turning test ($v_x=6.5\,\mathrm{m/s}, \omega_z=0.35\,\mathrm{rad/s}$) exposed dramatic differences (Figure F3 b). MHA maintained stable turning at a 24.2 m radius (close to the theoretical 18.6 m). In contrast, LSTM drifted by $1.8\times$, GRU by $2.2\times$, and HIM suffered catastrophic falls due to centrifugal force. MHA's self-attention selectively attends to key contact moments across the gait cycle, maintaining balance even under severe turning loads.

### 4.3 Effect of the Heading-Direction Reward (E2)
Reverting to conventional yaw-rate tracking severely degraded turning performance (Figure F4). The yaw-rate tracking policy widened its turning radius to 146.7 m (approx. $8\times$ theoretical), effectively running straight. It also maintained an upright torso without inward lean. In contrast, the proposed heading reward produced stable laps at a 24.2 m radius with a center drift of just 1.7 m (compared to 8.2 m for yaw tracking), while naturally discovering an inward bank angle exceeding 13 degrees.

### 4.4 Single Discriminator vs. Multi-AMP (E3)
Under a single shared discriminator, commanded in-place turning produced an actual yaw rate of only 0.08 rad/s against a 0.6 rad/s command. The double-support ratio surged to 97%, completely collapsing into a static standing posture. Without skill conditioning, the discriminator cannot distinguish standing from in-place stepping, destroying the incentive to take steps.

### 4.5 Real-Robot Deployment and Robustness
In official 100m track measurements, a lightweight prototype (60 kg) clocked flat 14.0 seconds, yielding an average speed of 7.14 m/s (~25.7 km/h) (Figure F5). A smaller humanoid (1.36 m, 40 kg) completed the 100m dash in 22 seconds (4.55 m/s) with the exact same architecture, confirming cross-platform versatility. In simulation disturbance push tests, recovery was 100% up to 5.5 m/s, but dropped to 56–72% at 6.5 m/s due to near-total torque saturation in hip and knee motors.

(b) In high-speed turning (6.5 m/s, 0.35 rad/s), MHA maintains a turning radius of 24.2 m close to theoretical (green dashed line), whereas GRU and LSTM drift widely outward, and HIM falls.

(a) Trajectories over 15 laps show yaw-rate tracking (blue) ballooning to a 146.7 m radius, whereas heading-direction tracking (red) accurately follows the 24.2 m circle. (d)(e) Posture comparisons show only the proposed method spontaneously leaning deeply inward to counteract centrifugal force.

sections.heading: Hardware Limits and Unknown Gaits at Extreme Speeds
sections.summary: Current experiments are limited to flat or gently rolling terrain, requiring exteroception for rough surfaces like stairs. Furthermore, top speeds hit actuator torque limits, beyond which unexplored hardware-optimized gaits without human reference data will be needed.
sections.details:
Despite impressive achievements, several clear limitations remain:

- Terrain Adaptation Limits: Training environments only included minor bumps and gentle slopes. Because locomotion relies purely on proprioception (blind locomotion), integrating exteroceptive vision (cameras or LiDAR) will be essential for stairs and rugged terrain.
- Actuator Torque Saturation: The primary bottleneck limiting top speed on real hardware is motor torque, not algorithmic capacity. At peak velocity, hip pitch and knee pitch actuators reach ~99% of torque limits, and ankle pitch reaches ~90%, leaving minimal control margin to reject external disturbances.
- Lack of Reference Motions at Extreme Velocities: When penalizing power consumption to protect motors, robots tend to discover non-human postures, such as crouching low and swinging arms wildly. However, no human motion capture data exists for sprinters running at extreme robotic speeds, leaving reference prior design at the limit an open question.

sections.heading: Dawn of Full-Scale Bipeds Sprinting and Carving Sharp Turns
sections.summary: Combining a causal MHA encoder, heading-direction rewards, and skill-conditioned Multi-AMP enabled zero-shot deployment of >7 m/s sprinting and aggressive cornering on a full-scale humanoid. Future work points toward visual integration and pushing top speeds even higher.
sections.details:
By integrating three foundational ideas—temporal history encoding via causal self-attention (MHA), a heading-direction reward immune to foot-strike yaw oscillations, and skill-conditioned Multi-AMP discriminators—this work achieved >25 km/h sprinting and sharp cornering with up to 25° trunk lean on a physical full-scale humanoid.

Bipedal control has historically faced a trade-off: robust but slow and unnatural, or natural and human-like but fragile and sluggish. Demonstrating that natural gait dynamics and extreme agility can coexist at sprint speeds is a significant milestone. Future research will build upon this framework, incorporating vision to tackle high-speed traversal across complex real-world terrains.

sections.heading: 100m Dash Measurements, Architecture, and Training Details
sections.summary: This appendix covers track timing methodologies, detailed layer structures for the MHA Actor, domain randomization ranges, and actuator delay modeling.
sections.details:
The appendix provides critical implementation details supporting the reliability of the experiments:

- Real 100m Dash Measurement: On a standard running track, 100 meters was measured with a tape measure, and run times were determined from video frame timestamps. The lightweight primary robot (60 kg) clocked flat 14.0 s (7.14 m/s), while a smaller 23-DoF robot (1.36 m, 40 kg) clocked 22.0 s (4.55 m/s).
- Complete Elimination of State Estimators: The Actor receives no base translational velocity observations, taking only trunk IMU angular velocity/attitude and joint encoder states as input (translational velocity is accessed solely by the Critic during training).
- MHA Actor Network Architecture: Proprioceptive tokens (56D) are mapped to 128D via a shared 2-layer MLP, with sinusoidal positional encodings added. They pass through a 1-layer, 2-head causal Transformer (hidden dim 256, GELU) and are temporally mean-pooled into a 128D summary. Concatenated with projected command embeddings, this passes through a 3-layer MLP ([512, 256, 128]) to predict target joint angles.
- Actuator Modeling: An implicit first-order delay model mimics the response of real BLDC motors, incorporating 0 to 4 steps (0–20 ms) of random communication latency. Natural frequencies of 2–5 Hz and damping ratios of 0.5–0.707 are modeled for legs and waist to minimize the sim-to-real dynamic gap.

takeaways: Proprioceptive feedback during ultra-high-speed sprinting contains severe high-frequency yaw oscillations; explicitly modeling temporal structures with modules like causal MHA is essential over flat MLPs.

When periodic gait dynamics induce natural trunk swaying, evaluating translational velocity heading rather than instantaneous yaw rate avoids artificial deceleration and induces dynamic leaning turns.
When learning multi-speed skills with AMP, separating discriminators per commanded skill is necessary to prevent mode collapse where static skills degenerate into frozen stances.

Instead of simply expanding network parameter counts, aligning policy architectures and reward formulations with physical frequency characteristics (high-frequency impacts vs. low-frequency heading) is key to sim-to-real success.
limitations: Relies purely on blind proprioceptive control, leaving the robot unable to negotiate stairs or severe uneven terrain without exteroceptive sensors like cameras or LiDAR.
Actuator torques reach near-total saturation (99% at peak speeds), leaving negligible control margin against high winds or heavy impact disturbances.
High-quality human motion capture data does not exist for extreme sprinting and aggressive cornering limits, leaving reference motion prior design in ultra-high-speed regimes an unresolved challenge.
